# Pembrokeshire Coast National Park

Scroll down


## A Wonder Filled Coast

**The Pembrokeshire Coast isn’t what you might expect from a National Park. It’s split into four parts, each one with its own quirks and charms.**

It’s one of the smallest of the UK’s National Parks but don’t let the size fool you, you’re at the gateway to a range of stunning landscapes. The quality coastline is backed by hills, estuaries, valleys and woodlands just waiting to be discovered.

With over 600 miles of public footpaths and bridleways, walking is an ideal way to discover the Pembrokeshire Coast’s scenery, wildlife and history.

Explore the amazing wildlife that makes its home on the Pembrokeshire Coast - not forgetting the exciting array of seasonal wildlife which also visits year after year.

Britain's only truly coastal National Park boasts a variety of beaches. Some are easy to reach and ideal for families, others are less accessible but offer peace and quiet.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/03.-Long-Form-Copy-Special-Qualities-1600X1600-1600x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

5 reasons why the Pembrokeshire Coast is a special place

The Pembrokeshire Coast is the only UK National Park which is primarily designated for its coastal landscape.

It’s one of the smallest UK National Parks, but has one of the most diverse landscapes, covering almost all the Pembrokeshire Coast, every offshore island, the Daugleddau estuary and large areas of the Preseli Hills and the Gwaun Valley.

It’s home to the Pembrokeshire Coast Path National Trail – a spectacular 186 mile (299 km) long National Trail covering some of the most varied coastal scenery in Britain.

It is ecologically one of the richest and most diverse parts of Wales and is recognised as of international importance for a wide range of high quality habitats and rare species.

The Park has a rich cultural and built heritage, being home to 286 Scheduled Ancient Monuments and 1234 listed buildings.

## Did you know?

Nowhere in the National Park is more than ten miles from the sea.

# The coast with the most

The Pembrokeshire Coast is the home of outdoor adventure for all, from high energy watersports to relaxing walks and wildlife watching, while there’s more to explore indoors if you want to escape the elements.

No visit is complete without a walk on the Pembrokeshire Coast Path, but you don’t have to be an experienced explorer to enjoy the route.

The Path passes all the area’s beautiful beaches, links with nearby footpaths and with some stretches accessible to wheelchair users and families with prams and pushchairs, it’s easier than ever to tick this off your bucket and spade list.

Walking the entire route is no mean feat – in fact, the total rise and fall of the Coast Path is over 35,000 feet – greater than the height of Mount Everest.

But there’s no rule to say you’ve got to walk it all. In fact, there are many different ways you can use the Path to discover the Park. You can reduce the route into a series of sections to suit your aims and ability.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/05.-Middle-Copy-Block-Kayaking-1800X1200-1800x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/06.-Getting-Around-1600x1600-1-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

The Pembrokeshire Coastal Bus Services help locals and visitors get to the coast without having to use a car, travelling along the coast to provide access to walks, beaches, boat trips, local villages and attractions.

# A Wonder Filled Coast

## Welcome to the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park

![Strumble Head Light house in Pembrokeshire Coast National Park](https://www.pembrokeshirecoast.wales/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/STRUMBLE-HEAD-LIGHT-HOUSE-2-scaled.jpg)

## Discover. Explore. Life is outside.

From miles of dazzling coastline to the wilds of the Preseli Hills, beautiful countryside and thriving wildlife make the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park one of the country’s top places to visit.

The Pembrokeshire Coast Path twists and turns along 186 miles of the most mind-blowing coastline in Britain - from rugged clifftops to wide-open beaches and winding estuaries.

From relaxing strolls and star gazing to high-octane hobbies like surfing and coasteering, you can find your happy place on the Pembrokeshire Coast.

Set off on a voyage of discovery and seek out the scenery, sands and rare species that make this corner of West Wales so spectacular!

# Pembrokeshire Coast National Park Pembrokeshire Coast National Park National park in Wales | Pembrokeshire Coast National Park | | --- | | _Parc Cenedlaethol Arfordir Penfro_( [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language")) | | [IUCN category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_protected_area_categories "IUCN protected area categories") V (protected landscape/seascape) | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Green_Bridge_of_Wales_1_-_Pembrokeshire_%282010%29.jpg/960px-Green_Bridge_of_Wales_1_-_Pembrokeshire_%282010%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Green_Bridge_of_Wales_1_-_Pembrokeshire_(2010).jpg)

Location of the national park in [Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire "Pembrokeshire"), [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") | | Location | [Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire "Pembrokeshire"), [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") | | Area | 629km2 (243sqmi) | | Established | 1952 | | Website | [www.pembrokeshirecoast.wales](https://www.pembrokeshirecoast.wales/)[![Edit this at Wikidata](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8a/OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg/20px-OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1893297#P856 "Edit this at Wikidata") | The **Pembrokeshire Coast National Park** ( [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language "Welsh language"): _Parc Cenedlaethol Arfordir Penfro_) is a [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_of_England_and_Wales "National Parks of England and Wales") in the county of [Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire "Pembrokeshire"), Wales. It was established in 1952 and includes most of the coast of the county, the upper reaches of [Milford Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Haven_Waterway "Milford Haven Waterway"), and the [Preseli Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preseli_Mountains "Preseli Mountains") in the north. When the creation of the national park was being considered in 1947, the "rock-bound coastline" of Pembrokeshire was described as "the most spectacular of its many attractions". The national park covers 420km (260 miles) of this coastline and a total of 650 square miles (1,700km2).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-1) It is one of three [national parks in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_Wales "National parks of Wales"), the others being the [Brecon Beacons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_Beacons_National_Park "Brecon Beacons National Park") (Bannau Brycheiniog) and [Snowdonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowdonia "Snowdonia") (Eryri). It is the only national park in the United Kingdom to consist largely of coastal landscapes.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-3) ## Establishment The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park was established in 1952 under the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949 "National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-4) The 1947 Hobhouse Report, the precursor to the Act, recommended the creation of the national park with boundaries similar to those ultimately adopted, although excluding the coast from [Tenby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenby "Tenby") to [Amroth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amroth "Amroth") and the part of the Preseli Hills around [Mynachlog-ddu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynachlog-ddu "Mynachlog-ddu").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-:4-5) Among other reasons for recommending designation, the report praised the northern coast between [Pen Caer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_Caer "Pen Caer") and [St David's Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_David's_Head "St David's Head") as "one of the best stretches of coastal scenery in the British Isles", noted the importance of the islands of [Grassholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassholm "Grassholm"), [Skomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skomer "Skomer"), and [Skokholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skokholm "Skokholm") to seabirds, and called Milford Haven one of the best examples of a [ria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria "Ria") in England and Wales. The challenges of designation included the military use of several areas, including [Castlemartin Training Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlemartin_Training_Area "Castlemartin Training Area"), and unsympathetic holiday development particularly at [Freshwater East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshwater_East "Freshwater East") and [Newgale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgale,_Pembrokeshire "Newgale, Pembrokeshire").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-:4-5) ## Landscape [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/St_Govans%27_chapel_-_geograph.org.uk_-_876068.jpg/500px-St_Govans%27_chapel_-_geograph.org.uk_-_876068.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Govans'_chapel_-_geograph.org.uk_-_876068.jpg) [St Govan's Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Govan's_Chapel "St Govan's Chapel") See also: [Geology of Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Pembrokeshire "Geology of Pembrokeshire") The National Park has a varied landscape of rugged [cliffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliff "Cliff"), sandy [beaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach "Beach"), wooded estuaries, wild inland hills, the moorland of the Preseli Hills and the wooded Gwaun valley. The total area is 629km2 (243sqmi). There are four distinct sections: clockwise these are the south Pembrokeshire coast, including [Caldey Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldey_Island "Caldey Island"); the [Daugleddau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daugleddau "Daugleddau") estuary; the [St Bride's Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bride's_Bay "St Bride's Bay") coast, including the coastal islands; and the [Preseli Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preseli_Hills "Preseli Hills"). The [geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology "Geology") of the area is of particular interest with many good exposures both inland and along the coast, exhibiting a variety of rock types and structural features such as [natural arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_arch "Natural arch"), [stacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(geology) "Stack (geology)"), [rock folding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fold_(geology) "Fold (geology)") and [sea caves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cave "Sea cave"). A stack of note is Elegug Stacks (_Creigiau Elegug_), two large detached pillars of limestone which in the spring provide valued nesting sites for razorbills and guillemots.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-6) In the north, the rocks of [Carn Llidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carn_Llidi "Carn Llidi"), Pen Beri and Garn Fawr, together with the extensive [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") on [Mynydd Carningli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynydd_Carningli "Mynydd Carningli") and [Mynydd Preseli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynydd_Preseli "Mynydd Preseli"), give an exposed and mountainous feel to the landscape, cut through by the wooded valleys of the [Gwaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Gwaun "River Gwaun") and [Nevern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afon_Nyfer "Afon Nyfer"). In the west, the National Park is dominated by the broad sweep of [St Bride's Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bride's_Bay "St Bride's Bay"), bounded at its northern end by [Ramsey Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey_Island "Ramsey Island"), near [St David's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_David's "St David's") peninsula, and at its southern end by [Skomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skomer "Skomer"). The southern coast is another contrast, with the limestone plateau and cliffs of the [Castlemartin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlemartin,_Pembrokeshire "Castlemartin, Pembrokeshire") peninsula, the steep-sided wooded valleys inland from [Amroth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amroth,_Pembrokeshire "Amroth, Pembrokeshire"); the [Bosherston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosherston "Bosherston") lakes — now, like much of the coastal strip, in the care of the [National Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trust_for_Places_of_Historic_Interest_or_Natural_Beauty "National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty") — and the tourist resorts of [Tenby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenby "Tenby") and [Saundersfoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saundersfoot "Saundersfoot"). Between the western and southern areas of the National Park lies the [Milford Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Haven "Milford Haven") waterway, where the tranquil Daugleddau estuary feeds into one of the finest natural deep water harbours in the world.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-pcnpa-7) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Pentre_Ifan_burial_chamber_-_geograph.org.uk_-_384085.jpg/500px-Pentre_Ifan_burial_chamber_-_geograph.org.uk_-_384085.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pentre_Ifan_burial_chamber_-_geograph.org.uk_-_384085.jpg) [Pentre Ifan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentre_Ifan "Pentre Ifan") The National Park includes many sites (such as [Pentre Ifan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentre_Ifan "Pentre Ifan")) of historic and archaeological importance and areas which are of national or international nature conservation significance in their own right, including 7 [Special Areas of Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Areas_of_Conservation "Special Areas of Conservation"), a [Marine Nature Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Nature_Reserve "Marine Nature Reserve"), 6 [national nature reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserve_(United_Kingdom) "National nature reserve (United Kingdom)") and 75 [Sites of Special Scientific Interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sites_of_Special_Scientific_Interest "Sites of Special Scientific Interest"). In 2011, _[National Geographic Traveler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Traveler "National Geographic Traveler")_ magazine voted Pembrokeshire the second best coastal destination in the world for [sustainable tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_tourism "Sustainable tourism").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-10) In January 2016 the Authority launched the "Changing Coasts" project to document the way the coastline has changed as a result of recent winter storms; the project invites visitors to submit photographs taken (at any time of day) from fixed points; a pilot study will be carried out at [Abereiddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abereiddy "Abereiddy").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-11) ## Pembrokeshire Coast Path Main article: [Pembrokeshire Coast Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_Path "Pembrokeshire Coast Path") The Pembrokeshire Coast Path is a designated [National Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trail "National Trail").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-12) It was established in 1970, and is 186 miles (299km) long, much of it at cliff-top level, with a total of 35,000 feet (11,000m) of ascent and descent. The southern end of the path is at [Amroth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amroth,_Pembrokeshire "Amroth, Pembrokeshire"). The northern end was regarded as being at [Poppit Sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poppit_Sands "Poppit Sands"), near [St. Dogmaels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Dogmaels "St. Dogmaels"), where the official plaque was sited;[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-PCPPath-13) however, the path now continues to St. Dogmaels,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-PembrokeshireCoast-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-15) where a new marker was unveiled in July 2009,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-16) and links with the [Ceredigion Coast Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceredigion_Coast_Path "Ceredigion Coast Path") to continue northwards[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-17) as part of the [Wales Coast Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales_Coast_Path "Wales Coast Path"), the 870-mile (1,400km) long-distance walking route around the whole coast of Wales from [Chepstow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chepstow "Chepstow") to [Queensferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensferry,_Flintshire "Queensferry, Flintshire"), which was officially opened in 2012.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire_Coast_National_Park#cite_note-BBCNews20111017-18) ## Administration The Park is managed by Pembrokeshire Coast National Park Authority, which has around 150 staff and a committee of 18 members. The Authority's purposes are to conserve and enhance the National Park, and encourage the public to enjoy and understand it. In pursuing these purposes, the authority has a duty to foster the social and economic well-being of the communities within its boundaries.
